# SaaS Is Dead: The Structural Shift from SaaS to Service-as-a-Software

> A structural analysis by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), AI Strategist,
> building on Sequoia Capital partner Julien Bek's "Services: The New
> Software" thesis: AI infrastructure investment requires ~$600B/year in
> ecosystem revenue that the $300B global SaaS market cannot mathematically
> supply, forcing AI applications to expand into the $6T services and
> labor market. The book argues SaaS is not dying but splitting into
> surviving Systems of Record and dying workflow-wrapper UIs, while a new
> category of "Autopilot" companies sells completed outcomes rather than
> software access. As stated in the book's closing lines: "サービス産業の
> $4.6兆の対象市場が、ソフトウェアの次の戦場になる。レースは始まった。"
> ("The services industry's $4.6T addressable market is software's next
> battleground. The race has begun.")

## Book Content

- [Full text (Japanese)](docs/jp/saas-is-dead_JP.md): 全10章・参考文献収録
- [Full text (English)](docs/en/saas-is-dead_EN.md): Complete English edition

## Key Facts (as stated in the book)

- The book cites Sequoia's David Cahn's "$600B Question" framework:
  starting from NVIDIA's projected revenue, doubling it for total
  data-center TCO, then doubling again for end-user gross margin
  requirements, yields ~$600B/year the AI ecosystem must generate in
  application-layer revenue — a gap the $300B global SaaS market cannot
  mathematically close
- The book documents the Feb 2026 "SaaSpocalypse": ~$2T in software-sector
  market cap lost within weeks, with the IGV software ETF down 22%
  year-to-date, Atlassian -35%, and Salesforce -28%, triggered by investor
  recognition of "seat compression" — AI agents replacing 500 SaaS seats
  with roughly 50 (Bain & Company estimate, -81% reduction)
- The book cites Sequoia partner Julien Bek's core framework distinguishing
  "Intelligence" (rule-based, pattern-driven, AI-replaceable) from
  "Judgement" (experience-based, intuition-driven, still human), with the
  prediction "today's judgement will become tomorrow's intelligence"
- The book cites Bek's "$1 vs $6" ratio: for every dollar spent on
  software, six dollars are spent on services — the structural reason
  "Autopilot" companies (selling completed outcomes) target a market 6x
  larger than "Copilot" companies (selling tools)
- The book profiles Autopilot pioneers with cited funding/valuation data:
  Sierra (Bret Taylor's company, $10B valuation, ARR $100M in 7 quarters,
  outcome-based pricing at $3-5 per resolved interaction vs. $15 for a
  human agent), Harvey ($11B valuation), Crosby, WithCoverage, Rillet, and
  Mercor
- The book notes current AI-company gross margins average ~25% against a
  SaaS benchmark of ~75%+, attributing the gap to inference cost, which it
  states has fallen roughly 10x per year (GPT-4 at $30/1M input tokens in
  2023 to DeepSeek R1 at $0.07/1M tokens)
- Ch.9 argues Japan's driver differs from the US: not cost-cutting but a
  labor shortage, citing Japan's working-age population falling from 87.3M
  (1995 peak) to 73.7M (2024) and METI's "2025 Digital Cliff" warning of
  ¥12 trillion in annual economic loss from unmodernized legacy IT systems
- The book notes Klarna's initial claim of full AI replacement of
  Salesforce/Workday was later reported as a hybrid reality — partial SaaS
  replacement supplemented by internal AI, not pure AI substitution

## Author & Full Catalog

This book is one of 20+ open-source books by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史),
AI Strategist & Business Designer at Sun Asterisk Inc., Founder of Leading.AI.
The book cross-references the author's Depth & Velocity methodology,
mapping its 10:80:10 model directly onto the Intelligence/Judgement
framework for building Autopilot companies in Japan.

> **Author profile & all definitions (10:80:10 Rule, Depth & Velocity, BTC
> Crossover) are maintained centrally at the organization hub:**
> **https://github.com/Leading-AI-IO**
